30-001.r: Number of Judges in a High Court → decided by the President; each HC has a Chief Justice and such other Judges as the President appoints (Article 216).
30-001.t: Not Parliament or the CM: the President fixes High Court strength.

30-002.r: Every High Court Judge → appointed by President by warrant under hand and seal (Article 217(1)), not by Governor; HCs hear second appeals and PILs.

30-003.r: Transfer of a High Court Judge → by President after consulting CJI (Article 222); Third Judges case (1998): CJI consults collegium of four senior-most SC Judges.

30-004.r: Additional and acting Judges → appointed in High Courts (Article 224), e.g. for temporary increase in business or arrears of work.

30-005.r: High Court Judges' salaries and allowances → Consolidated Fund of the State (Article 202(3)(d)); their pensions → Consolidated Fund of India (Article 112(3)(d)).
30-005.h: Salary from the State, pension from India.
hi: Consolidated Fund of the State (राज्य की संचित निधि)

30-007.r: High Court Judge retires at 62 (Article 217(1)), fixed by 15th Amendment (1963), earlier 60; 114th Amendment Bill (2010) to raise it to 65 did not pass.

30-009.r: India has 25 High Courts; Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh share one; NCT of Delhi is the only UT with a separate High Court of its own (Article 214).

30-010.r: High Courts → 25 at present; 7 have jurisdiction over more than one State/UT; UTs of Delhi and J&K have own High Courts; HC Judges retire at 62.
30-010.c: Option (a) reflects the older position (eighteen High Courts, three serving more than one State; judges retire at 62). Statement 3 was always false, as Delhi has its own High Court. There are now 25.

30-011.r: High Courts in India → 21 when the question was asked; 25 at present.
30-011.c: No answer printed (*): the count changed from 21 to 25, so no option is current.

30-012.r: HC jurisdiction over UTs: Andaman & Nicobar → Calcutta; Chandigarh → Punjab & Haryana; Puducherry → Madras (Chennai); Lakshadweep → Kerala; Delhi has its own.
30-012.h: Islands: Andaman goes to Calcutta, Lakshadweep to Kerala.

30-013.r: Bombay High Court → covers Maharashtra, Goa and UTs of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu.

30-014.r: High Courts over more than one State (UTs excluded) → 3: Gauhati (Arunachal, Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram), Bombay (Maharashtra, Goa), Punjab & Haryana.

30-015.r: Manipur → had no High Court of its own when asked (under Gauhati High Court); High Court of Manipur set up March 2013.
30-015.c: No answer printed (*): Manipur now has its own High Court, so no option is correct today.

30-016.r: Three new North-East High Courts → Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura (set up January 2013, working from March 2013).

30-017.r: Largest number of Benches → Bombay High Court (book also accepts Gauhati); MP High Court seat Jabalpur, Benches at Indore and Gwalior; Calcutta HC circuit benches at Port Blair, Jalpaiguri.

30-018.r: Advisory jurisdiction (Article 143) → Supreme Court only; High Courts have original, appellate and supervisory jurisdiction.

30-019.r: High Court Chief Justice acting in administrative capacity → subject to the writ jurisdiction of any other Judge of that High Court.

30-020.r: Certiorari → superior court orders an inferior court to send up the record of a case for review, usually to overrule its judgment.

30-021.r: Writ of Prohibition → issued by Supreme Court or High Court to a lower court or tribunal, stopping proceedings beyond its jurisdiction.

30-022.r: Certiorari → higher court calls up a case with all decisions and records from a subordinate court to examine and review it.

30-023.r: Writ of Prohibition → issued while proceedings are pending, when a lower court hears a case outside its jurisdiction.

30-024.r: Wilful disobedience of court orders and derogatory language about judges → Contempt of Court; judiciary needs punitive powers, but R does not explain A.

30-025.r: Mandamus → not against a private body unless it has a public duty; lies against a Government company; any public-minded person can seek Quo Warranto.

30-026.r: High Court writs (Article 226) → for Fundamental Rights and other rights (constitutional, statutory); Supreme Court writs (Article 32) only for Part III rights.

30-027.r: High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and any other matter (Article 226); Supreme Court only for Fundamental Rights (Article 32) → HCs better placed; R explains A.

30-028.r: HC Judge removed in the same way as SC Judge (Article 217(1)(b) with Article 124(4)); 'retired HC Judge cannot plead in any court' is false (Article 220).

30-029.r: High Court Judge resigns by writing to the President (Article 217(1)(a)).
30-029.t: Not to the Governor or the High Court's Chief Justice.

30-030.r: Justice Soumitra Sen (Calcutta HC) → Rajya Sabha passed impeachment motion in 2011 (misappropriation of funds); he resigned 1 September 2011 before Lok Sabha took it up.

30-031.r: Babri Mosque/Ramjanmabhoomi case before Allahabad High Court → a Title Suit (two communities claiming the same land and property).

30-032.r: Allahabad High Court (Rahmatullah vs State of UP, 1994) → triple 'Talaq' divorce illegal, violates Articles 14, 15; now barred by Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.

30-033.r: Rajeev Gupta → Chief Justice of Chhattisgarh High Court from 2 February 2008; earlier Chief Justice of Uttarakhand High Court.

30-034.r: Justice H.R. Khanna, Chairman of 8th Law Commission (80th report) → at least one-third of each High Court's Judges should be from other States.

30-035.r: Term 'District Judge' → Article 233 (appointment of District Judges).

30-036.r: 'District Judge' (Article 236(a)) includes city civil court judge, additional/joint/assistant district judge, small cause court chief judge, chief presidency magistrate, sessions judges; not Tribunal judges.

30-037.r: District Judge → highest judicial authority in the district, with judicial, administrative and supervisory powers; appointed by Governor consulting High Court (Article 233).

30-038.r: Advocates Act, 1961 → one class 'advocates' incl. government law officers, legal firms, corporate lawyers, patent attorneys; Bar Councils frame rules on legal education and law college recognition.

30-039.r: Prisons → State subject (entry 4, State List); governed by Prisons Act, 1894, which gave Provincial (now State) Governments rule-making power; both true, II explains I.

30-041.r: Lok Adalat → settles pre-litigation and pending cases, civil and criminal; works on consent of both parties; members not only judicial officers; all three statements false.

30-042.r: Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 → Gram Nyayalaya has both civil and criminal jurisdiction (Section 11); local social workers can act as conciliators (Section 27).

30-043.r: Mobile court → idea of Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam; first one in August 2007, Mewat district, Haryana, inaugurated by CJI K.G. Balakrishnan.

31-001.r: Centre-State relations (Part XI) → shaped by Constitutional provisions, the planning process, conflict of political interests and desire to dominate (all four).

31-002.r: Centre-State relations depend on Constitutional provisions, conventions and practices, judicial interpretations and mechanisms for dialogue (all four).

31-003.r: Federal polity involves Union-State relations, relations among States, mechanisms for cooperation and mechanisms for solving disputes (all four).

31-004.r: Centre's control over States in the planning process → termed 'Municipal Relations'.

31-005.r: Centre-to-State resource transfer now → tax sharing (Finance Commission, Article 280), grants-in-aid, centrally sponsored schemes; Gadgil formula plan transfers no longer used.

31-006.r: Union-State relations → Part XI: Legislative (Articles 245-255) and Administrative (Articles 256-263). Part III → Fundamental Rights; IV → DPSP; VI → States.

31-007.r: Legislative relations → Part XI, Articles 245-255; Seventh Schedule lists: Union 97 (now 98), State 66 (now 59), Concurrent 47 (now 52) subjects.

31-008.r: Distribution of legislative power → Article 245 (extent of laws by Parliament and State Legislatures) and Article 246 (subjects in Union, State, Concurrent Lists).
